title: Beyond Scheduling: Closing the Gaps That Lead to Missed Care
summary: Missed care often starts after the visit. See how patient engagement and proactive outreach can close critical care gaps.
body_markdown:
## When Follow-ups Don’t Follow Through


Sarah has type 2 diabetes, and today she has an appointment with her doctor. She is told that she needs to see an endocrinologist, undergo further blood tests, and possibly start taking a new medication. However, after her appointment, she doesn’t receive any reminders or follow-ups as to what she needs to do next. She also doesn’t check the portal to monitor recommendations from her initial visit, so her referral sits unread. As a result of her inaction, her condition deteriorates, and she’s rushed to the emergency room.


## The Root Problems Behind This Scenario


Failed patient and provider follow-through is more common than many people realize. If there were a simple fix, it would probably already be in place. The truth is that making the patient journey work smoothly depends on many things coming together.


**Disconnected systems**


One of the biggest issues is the lack of connection between the different tools, platforms, systems, and data sources used across large healthcare networks. These systems often do not communicate properly with one another. Because so many different people, teams, and providers are involved in supporting a patient, information often stays trapped in separate systems. When that happens, the patient journey starts to break down. At the same time, technology is not always being used as well as it could be to keep patients informed, updated, and clear on what they need to do next.


**Poor handling of patient data and AI risks**


Another issue is how healthcare organizations manage patient data. Healthcare providers need to think carefully about how medical information is handled and protected if they’re to remain compliant with regulations such as HIPAA. Simply applying AI to a problem and expecting it to solve everything is both naive and risky. If not used properly, AI can create risks around sensitive patient data.


**No clear plan for patient engagement**


Finally, many healthcare organizations still do not have a clear strategy for how patients should be encouraged and supported to use the tools available to them. This includes everything from booking appointments to managing follow-ups and ongoing care. Too often, patients are given access to digital tools without being shown how to use them properly or, more importantly, why they matter. Without clear guidance or education, patients are far less likely to make full use of self-service options and stay engaged in their care.


## What Healthcare Organizations Are Doing and Why It’s Not Enough


Healthcare organizations are trying to mitigate these challenges, but not enough is being done to resolve them.


While nearly[90% of medical practices](https://www.healthdatamanagement.com/articles/most-practices-using-automated-appointment-reminders-mgma-finds?) use automated appointment reminders to reduce no-shows and improve utilization, a 2024 national poll showed that[37% of medical groups](https://prod.mgma.com/mgma-stat/patient-no-shows-still-an-issue-despite-more-automated-reminders?) reported year-over-year increases in patient no-show rates.


A UK mental health service[reduced DNA (Did Not Attend) rates by 33%](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12242212/?) after implementing SMS reminders, but a broader, more comprehensive solution is needed.3 Analysis of 2024 NHS trust FOI responses estimated that 11.8 million appointments were missed (DNAs) across NHS trusts, with an[estimated cost of £1.9 billion](https://www.esendex.co.uk/blog/post/cost-of-missed-nhs-appointments/?) to the NHS. On their own, one provider’s actions are not enough to make a difference.


## What a Smarter Approach Looks Like in Practice


A possible solution is to look at two ways a proactive, intelligent appointment reminder and patient follow-through experience could come to life. The first is from the healthcare organization side. In Sarah’s case, that would mean the hospital system playing a much more active role after her appointment. Instead of relying on her to log into a portal, remember every next step, and manage the follow-up on her own, the system could use AI to act earlier and more proactively.


In practice, that could mean the hospital could have an AI agent or a group of agents working in the background across each patient’s journey. These agents could identify when a referral has not been opened, when follow-up tests have not been booked, or when a patient has not responded after a consultation. Rather than waiting for the problem to grow, the system could send reminders, prompt the patient to take the next step, flag risks to care teams, and help close the gaps that often lead to missed care. The goal would not be to replace people, but to make sure patients do not fall through the cracks simply because no one followed up at the right time.


The second way this experience could happen is from the patient’s side. Instead of the hospital leading the process, the patient could have their own AI assistant helping them manage their healthcare. In that model, the AI would act more like a personal guide. It could help the patient understand what the doctor recommended, keep track of appointments, explain what actions need to happen next, and bring everything together in one place. Rather than depending on multiple systems and portals, the patient would have a tool that helps them make sense of their care journey in a way that feels clearer and easier to manage.


This raises an important question: which of these two approaches would patients find more useful and trustworthy? Some people may prefer to stay in control and use their own AI assistant to manage their care in a way that feels personal and independent. Others may value proactive support from the hospital system, especially if it helps reduce stress and makes it easier to stay on top of important next steps. For many patients, the most effective approach may not be one or the other, but a combination of both. The hospital system can play a stronger role in preventing breakdowns in follow-up, while the patient also has access to a tool that helps them stay informed, organized, and engaged in their own care.


What matters most is that the AI-support experience feels supportive, timely, and trustworthy. Whether the help comes from the healthcare organization, the patient’s own AI, or a combination of both, the real opportunity is to create a model of care that is more connected, more responsive, and much less likely to let patients slip through unnoticed.


## CASE STUDY


A leading hospital found that many cancer patients arriving for chemotherapy appointments were unable to proceed with treatment because side effects or health concerns had not been identified in advance. This created unnecessary cancellations, wasted clinical capacity, and a poor experience for patients.


The hospital introduced proactive patient outreach before treatment, assessing symptoms and escalating concerns to care teams before appointments. This helped increase treatment adherence by 14%, reduce the length of stay by 25%, and cut treatment side effects by up to 75%.


[Read the full case study.](https://www.concentrix.com/insights/case-studies/revolutionizing-cancer-care-coordination/)


## What This Requires in Practice (Solution Layers)


Closing the gaps between appointments and follow-up care requires more than standalone reminders. It requires three connected layers that engage patients at the right moments, enable intelligent support, and integrate the systems and data behind the care journey.


When these layers work together, the impact shows up across three areas:


- **Access and experience** : Lower no-show rates, higher visit preparedness, improved post-visit CSAT and NPS.
- **Operational efficiency** : Fewer post-visit inbound calls, less rework and repeat outreach, higher self-service resolution rates.
- **Continuity and retention** : Better follow-through on next steps, higher digital tool adoption, and stronger patient and member loyalty.


One important limitation is that appointment scheduling, on its own, is only one part of the overall experience. It may work very well as a single interaction, but that alone does not make the experience truly patient-centered.


If scheduling is not connected to everything that comes before and after it, it remains an isolated moment in a much bigger journey. A patient may be able to book an appointment easily, but if follow-up steps are unclear, referrals are missed, test results are disconnected, or communication breaks down afterwards, the overall experience still fails.


That is why the real challenge is connecting each part of the journey to create an experience that feels seamless, consistent, and supportive from start to finish.
